requirements:
R1. Implement in Rust as a SINGLE source file that compiles with `rustc --edition 2024`, std only. Do not include a main function, inner attributes (`#![...]`), or inner documentation (`//!`). Output ONLY the Rust source code inside ```rust fences.

R2. Expose an opaque `pub struct Big` with private representation, implementing Clone, Debug, PartialEq and Eq. Values are arbitrary-precision signed integers. No traits beyond these are required.

R3. Expose `pub enum Error { Empty, SignOnly, InvalidDigit { index: usize }, Separator { index: usize }, LeadingZero { index: usize }, TooManyDigits { limit: usize, index: usize } }`, implementing Clone, Debug, PartialEq and Eq. Use exactly these variants and field types.

R4. Provide `pub fn parse(text: &str, max_digits: usize) -> Result<Self, Error>` as an associated function of Big. Parsing is decimal.

R5. Only at byte 0, one optional ASCII `+` or `-` is accepted. The rest is the magnitude. Minus makes nonzero values negative. No trimming or whitespace is allowed; a second sign is an invalid digit.

R6. The empty string returns Error::Empty.

R7. An allowed sign with no following bytes returns Error::SignOnly. This does not apply to a disallowed sign.

R8. The only valid digits are ASCII 0 through 9. Non-ASCII characters, whitespace, punctuation and misplaced signs are invalid bytes. Offsets in every error are zero-based UTF-8 BYTE offsets into the original text, including any sign.

R9. ASCII `_` is the only separator. It is valid only if its immediate preceding and following bytes in the magnitude are both valid digits. A leading, trailing or doubled underscore is malformed. Report Error::Separator { index } at the first malformed underscore, after the invalid-digit scan succeeds.

R10. Before validating underscores, scan ALL magnitude bytes for invalid digits, ignoring underscores. If there are any, return Error::InvalidDigit { index } for the leftmost invalid byte. For a non-ASCII character this is its first UTF-8 byte.

R11. InvalidDigit takes precedence over Separator anywhere in the input, even when the malformed underscore occurs first. After a successful invalid-byte scan, the leftmost malformed underscore wins over all digit-count or leading-zero errors.

R12. After lexical and separator validation, if there is more than one magnitude digit and its first digit is zero, return Error::LeadingZero { index } at that first digit. Ignore separators in counting digits. A single zero is accepted.

R13. After leading-zero validation, count magnitude digits, excluding sign and underscores. If this count exceeds max_digits, return Error::TooManyDigits { limit: max_digits, index } at the first excess digit (digit number max_digits + 1). Zero counts as one digit, so max_digits=0 rejects even zero. The limit is local to this parse call.

R14. The complete parse error precedence is Empty, SignOnly, InvalidDigit, Separator, LeadingZero, TooManyDigits. Only applicable errors participate. Within each indexed error use the offset specified above; never stop early merely because a lower-priority error is already visible.

R15. There is no machine-integer bound and no implicit digit limit; accept every otherwise-valid input whose digit count is within max_digits. Parsing and arithmetic must be exact for arbitrarily large integers within available memory.

R16. Equality compares numerical values, independent of sign spelling, separators, formatting or parse limit. There is exactly one zero value; `-0` and `+0` both equal `0`. Cloning preserves equality.

R17. Provide `pub fn format(&self, min_digits: usize, group: usize) -> String`. Output is decimal. This is a method of Big.

R18. Format the absolute magnitude with no unnecessary leading zeros, except pad on the left with zero digits until it has at least min_digits digits. Zero always has at least one digit, even when min_digits=0. min_digits is a minimum, not a truncation width.

R19. After padding, if group>0 insert `_` between groups of exactly group magnitude digits counted from the RIGHT. The leftmost group may be shorter; never emit a leading or trailing underscore. group=0 disables grouping; group=1 separates every digit. Padding digits participate in grouping.

R20. Formatting prepends `-` exactly for negative values, outside the grouped magnitude; never emit `+` or a negative zero. Padding/grouping are presentation only; padded output is not necessarily a valid parse input under the leading-zero rule.

R21. Provide `pub fn cmp_value(&self, rhs: &Self) -> std::cmp::Ordering`. Compare numerical values with all negative values below zero and positives, reversing magnitude order for two negatives.

R22. Provide `pub fn add(&self, rhs: &Self) -> Self` for exact signed addition. A carry may create arbitrarily many additional digits.

R23. Provide `pub fn sub(&self, rhs: &Self) -> Self` for exact signed subtraction; negative results are valid.

R24. All methods leave their operands unchanged. Returned arithmetic values have the same canonical numerical equality and formatting behavior as parsed values. No operation retains a parse limit or an original text spelling.

R25. Provide `pub fn neg(&self) -> Self`, returning the additive inverse; negating zero yields the same canonical zero.

R26. Provide `pub fn signum(&self) -> i8`, returning exactly -1, 0, or 1 for negative, zero, or positive values, respectively.

R27. Provide `pub fn mul(&self, rhs: &Self) -> Self` for exact signed multiplication; signs multiply normally and multiplying by zero always yields canonical zero.

R28. Cancellation in addition/subtraction, and all other routes to zero, must erase the negative sign. In particular x + (-x), x - x, and zero * negative are indistinguishable from parsed zero.

R29. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, negation and comparison work for all sign combinations. In particular subtracting a negative adds its magnitude, and a negative times a negative is positive.
